## Every lecture: key | course | min | title | takeaway

### MATH 110 — Unit I — Essence of Linear Algebra (3Blue1Brown)
math110.0.0 | MATH 110 | 10 | Vectors | Everything in linear algebra is built from exactly two operations: adding vectors and scaling them.
math110.0.1 | MATH 110 | 10 | Linear combinations, span, and basis vectors | Coordinates are scalars applied to a chosen basis, and the span is everything those scalars can reach.
math110.0.2 | MATH 110 | 11 | Linear transformations and matrices | A linear transformation is fully determined by where the basis vectors land — and that is all a matrix records.
math110.0.3 | MATH 110 | 10 | Matrix multiplication as composition | Matrix multiplication is doing one transformation after another, which is why order matters and why the rows-times-columns rule looks the way it does.
math110.0.4 | MATH 110 | 5 | Three-dimensional linear transformations | Nothing changes in three dimensions: the transformation is still completely described by where the basis vectors land.
math110.0.5 | MATH 110 | 10 | The determinant | The determinant is the factor by which a transformation scales area, and its sign says whether space was flipped.
math110.0.6 | MATH 110 | 12 | Inverse matrices, column space and null space | Solving $A\vec{x}=\vec{v}$ asks which vector lands on $\vec{v}$, and the determinant decides whether that question has one answer.
math110.0.7 | MATH 110 | 4 | Nonsquare matrices as transformations between dimensions | The shape of a matrix is not bookkeeping: the columns count the input's dimensions and the rows count the output's.
math110.0.8 | MATH 110 | 14 | Dot products and duality | Every linear map from space down to the number line is secretly a vector, and dotting with that vector is applying the map.
math110.0.9 | MATH 110 | 9 | Cross products | The 2D cross product is a signed area; the 3D one is a vector whose length is that area.
math110.0.10 | MATH 110 | 13 | Cross products in the light of linear transformations | The cross product is the dual vector of a volume function, which is why a determinant computes it and why it comes out perpendicular.
math110.0.11 | MATH 110 | 12 | Cramer's rule, explained geometrically | Each coordinate of the unknown vector is an area, and every area scales by the determinant — that is the whole of Cramer's rule.
math110.0.12 | MATH 110 | 13 | Change of basis | A matrix whose columns are someone else's basis vectors translates their coordinates into yours; its inverse goes the other way.
math110.0.13 | MATH 110 | 17 | Eigenvectors and eigenvalues | An eigenvector is a direction the transformation only stretches, never turns, and its eigenvalue is that stretch.
math110.0.14 | MATH 110 | 13 | A quick trick for computing eigenvalues | The trace and the determinant hand you the mean and the product of the eigenvalues, and two numbers are pinned down by those.
math110.0.15 | MATH 110 | 17 | Abstract vector spaces | A vector is anything you can sensibly add and scale, and every result in linear algebra applies to all of them at once.

### MATH 110 — Unit II — MIT 18.06, Gilbert Strang (full course)
math110.1.0 | MATH 110 | 40 | The Geometry of Linear Equations | Every linear system has a row picture and a column picture, and the column picture is the one that survives into higher dimensions.
math110.1.1 | MATH 110 | 48 | Elimination with Matrices | Elimination is a sequence of row operations, and every row operation is multiplication on the left by one very simple matrix.
math110.1.2 | MATH 110 | 47 | Multiplication and Inverse Matrices | Matrix multiplication is one operation with five readings, and the one that pays later is column times row, because it builds a matrix out of a single rank-one piece.
math110.1.3 | MATH 110 | 48 | Factorization into A = LU | Elimination undone is tidier than elimination done: the multipliers drop straight into $L$, so the factorisation $A=LU$ costs nothing beyond the elimination already performed.
math110.1.4 | MATH 110 | 48 | Transposes, Permutations, Spaces R^n | A subspace is any set of vectors you cannot escape by adding or scaling, which is why every one of them contains the zero vector.
math110.1.5 | MATH 110 | 46 | Column Space and Nullspace | The column space says which right-hand sides are reachable; the null space says how many ways each reachable one can be reached.
math110.1.6 | MATH 110 | 43 | Solving Ax = 0: Pivot Variables, Special Solutions | Elimination does not change the null space, and what it leaves behind — the pivot columns — tells you exactly how many free choices the solutions have.
math110.1.7 | MATH 110 | 47 | Solving Ax = b: Row Reduced Form R | Every solution of $A\vec{x}=\vec{b}$ is one particular solution plus anything from the null space, and the rank alone decides whether there are none, one, or infinitely many.
math110.1.8 | MATH 110 | 50 | Independence, Basis, and Dimension | A basis is the set of vectors that is neither redundant nor short, and every basis for a given space turns out to have the same size.
math110.1.9 | MATH 110 | 49 | The Four Fundamental Subspaces | A matrix carries four subspaces, and their dimensions are fixed by the rank alone: $r$, $n-r$, $r$ and $m-r$.
math110.1.10 | MATH 110 | 46 | Matrix Spaces; Rank 1; Small World Graphs | Rank-one matrices are exactly the products $\vec{u}\vec{v}^{T}$, and every matrix of rank $r$ is a sum of $r$ of them — which is why they are the building blocks.
math110.1.11 | MATH 110 | 48 | Graphs, Networks, Incidence Matrices | An incidence matrix turns a graph into linear algebra, and then each of the four subspaces says something you could have read off the picture.
math110.1.12 | MATH 110 | 48 | Quiz 1 Review | A revision hour for chapters 1 to 3, and the questions are mostly worked backwards: from a stated answer to the matrix that produced it.
math110.1.13 | MATH 110 | 50 | Orthogonal Vectors and Subspaces | The row space and the null space are not merely different subspaces: they meet at right angles and between them account for the whole of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
math110.1.14 | MATH 110 | 49 | Projections onto Subspaces | Projection is what you do when $A\vec{x}=\vec{b}$ has no solution: replace $\vec{b}$ by the nearest point of the column space and solve that instead.
math110.1.15 | MATH 110 | 48 | Projection Matrices and Least Squares | Least squares is a projection: the best line is the one whose predicted values are the projection of the data onto the column space.
math110.1.16 | MATH 110 | 49 | Orthogonal Matrices and Gram-Schmidt | With an orthonormal basis every formula in this chapter collapses, and Gram-Schmidt is the procedure that manufactures one from any independent set.
math110.1.17 | MATH 110 | 49 | Properties of Determinants | Three properties define the determinant completely, and everything else — including the formula and the test for invertibility — is deduced from them.
math110.1.18 | MATH 110 | 53 | Determinant Formulas and Cofactors | Splitting every row into its coordinates turns the three properties into a formula with $n!$ terms, and grouping those terms by the first row gives cofactors.
math110.1.19 | MATH 110 | 51 | Cramer's Rule, Inverse Matrix, and Volume | The determinant turns three algorithms into formulas — the inverse, the solution, and the volume — and only the last of the three is worth computing that way.
math110.1.20 | MATH 110 | 51 | Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors | An eigenvector is a direction the matrix does not turn, and finding one starts by making $A-\lambda I$ singular.
math110.1.21 | MATH 110 | 52 | Diagonalization and Powers of A | Put the eigenvectors in the columns of $S$ and $A$ becomes diagonal, which turns the hundredth power of a matrix into the hundredth power of $n$ numbers.
math110.1.22 | MATH 110 | 51 | Differential Equations and exp(At) | Exponentials do for differential equations exactly what powers did for difference equations, and the eigenvalues decide the fate of the solution before you compute anything.
math110.1.23 | MATH 110 | 51 | Markov Matrices; Fourier Series | A Markov matrix always has $\lambda=1$, and the eigenvector that goes with it is the population the system settles into.
math110.1.24 | MATH 110 | 48 | Quiz 2 Review | A revision hour for orthogonality, determinants and the start of eigenvalues, where most questions are quick if you notice which structure applies.
math110.1.25 | MATH 110 | 44 | Symmetric Matrices and Positive Definiteness | Symmetry buys two things nothing else does: the eigenvalues are real and the eigenvectors can be chosen perpendicular, so $A = Q\Lambda Q^{T}$.
math110.1.26 | MATH 110 | 48 | Complex Matrices; Fast Fourier Transform | Every inner product gains a conjugate when the numbers go complex, and the Fourier matrix — the most important complex matrix — factors so well that its transform runs in $n\log n$.
math110.1.27 | MATH 110 | 51 | Positive Definite Matrices and Minima | Positive definite means $\vec{x}^{T}A\vec{x} \gt 0$ for every non-zero $\vec{x}$, which is the matrix version of a positive second derivative — the test for a minimum.
math110.1.28 | MATH 110 | 46 | Similar Matrices and Jordan Form | Two matrices are similar when $B = M^{-1}AM$, and similarity preserves the eigenvalues exactly while scrambling the eigenvectors.
math110.1.29 | MATH 110 | 40 | Singular Value Decomposition | The SVD finds an orthonormal basis of the row space that $A$ carries to an orthonormal basis of the column space, which no single set of eigenvectors can do.
math110.1.30 | MATH 110 | 49 | Linear Transformations and Their Matrices | A linear transformation exists without coordinates; choosing a basis for the inputs and one for the outputs is what turns it into a matrix.
math110.1.31 | MATH 110 | 50 | Change of Basis; Image Compression | Compression is a change of basis: rewrite the image in a basis where most coefficients are tiny, then throw those away.
math110.1.32 | MATH 110 | 47 | Quiz 3 Review | A revision hour for chapter 6, where nearly every question is answered by naming the family a matrix belongs to and quoting what that family does to its eigenvalues.
math110.1.33 | MATH 110 | 42 | Left and Right Inverses; Pseudoinverse | Restricted to the row space, every matrix is invertible onto its column space — and the pseudoinverse is that inverse, extended by zero on the null spaces.
math110.1.34 | MATH 110 | 43 | Final Course Review | The last hour is the whole course read backwards: given an answer, name the fact about $m$, $n$ and $r$ — or about the family of matrix — that produces it.

### MATH 120 — Unit I — Essence of Calculus (3Blue1Brown)
math120.0.0 | MATH 120 | 17 | The essence of calculus | Hard problems become sums of many small quantities, those sums become areas under graphs, and derivatives are how you find those areas.
math120.0.1 | MATH 120 | 17 | The paradox of the derivative | "Instantaneous rate of change" is an oxymoron, and the derivative is the clever construction that gets the meaning without the contradiction.
math120.0.2 | MATH 120 | 18 | Derivative formulas through geometry | Derivative formulas are not rules to memorise: draw what the function literally means, nudge the input, and read the answer off the picture.
math120.0.3 | MATH 120 | 16 | Visualizing the chain rule and product rule | There are only three ways to combine functions — add, multiply, compose — so three rules cover every expression, however monstrous.
math120.0.4 | MATH 120 | 14 | What's so special about Euler's number e? | Every exponential is proportional to its own derivative, and $e$ is simply the base for which that proportionality constant is 1.
math120.0.5 | MATH 120 | 16 | Implicit differentiation, what's going on here? | Implicit differentiation stops being strange once you read $2x\,dx + 2y\,dy$ as how much a two-variable expression changes under a step $(dx, dy)$.
math120.0.6 | MATH 120 | 18 | Limits, L'Hôpital's rule, and epsilon delta definitions | Limits exist to avoid talking about infinitely small changes, and once you have them the derivative can turn around and evaluate limits.
math120.0.7 | MATH 120 | 21 | Integration and the fundamental theorem of calculus | The integral is the limit of a sum of thin rectangles, and you evaluate it by finding an antiderivative and looking at just two inputs.
math120.0.8 | MATH 120 | 13 | What does area have to do with slope? | Averaging a continuous quantity is an integral divided by a width — and reading that as an average slope explains why antiderivatives solve integrals at all.
math120.0.9 | MATH 120 | 6 | Higher order derivatives | The second derivative is the derivative of the derivative — visually it is curvature, and physically it is acceleration.
math120.0.10 | MATH 120 | 22 | Taylor series | Taylor series translate derivative information at a single point into approximation information near that point, by matching one derivative per coefficient.
math120.0.11 | MATH 120 | 14 | The other way to visualize derivatives | Read a function as a transformation of the number line and the derivative becomes a local stretch factor — a view that survives into contexts where graphs do not.

### MATH 120 — Unit II — MIT 18.01, David Jerison (full course)
math120.1.0 | MATH 120 | 52 | Rate of Change | The derivative is the slope of the tangent line, defined as the limit of secant slopes — and the difference quotient is the formula that makes it computable.
math120.1.1 | MATH 120 | 53 | Limits | A derivative is a rate of change, and making that rigorous means separating left and right limits — which is also what makes continuity definable.
math120.1.2 | MATH 120 | 50 | Derivatives | Both trig derivatives come from two limits at zero, and those two limits come from one geometric fact: short pieces of curve are nearly straight.
math120.1.3 | MATH 120 | 46 | Chain Rule | Product, quotient and chain rules are proved the same way — write the change, add and subtract a middle term, divide by $\Delta x$ — and the chain rule is the one that sets you free.
math120.1.4 | MATH 120 | 49 | Implicit Differentiation | Differentiate the equation you were given instead of solving it first, and both fractional powers and every inverse function fall out.
math120.1.5 | MATH 120 | 48 | Exponential and Log | There is exactly one base whose exponential is its own derivative, and defining $e$ to be that base is what makes every other exponential and every logarithm differentiable.
math120.1.6 | MATH 120 | 51 | Exam 1 Review | Exam 1 is Unit I in two columns: five general rules that combine functions, and a memorised list of specific derivatives — plus the ability to read the definition of the derivative backwards.
math120.1.7 | MATH 120 | 47 | Linear and Quadratic Approximations | Replacing a hard function by its tangent line near one point is the whole of linear approximation, and the second derivative supplies the curvature the line cannot see.
math120.1.8 | MATH 120 | 52 | Curve Sketching | The sign of $f'$ says which way the curve goes and the sign of $f''$ says which way it bends — but the ends of the graph, the ones off the screen, are the part only you can supply.
math120.1.9 | MATH 120 | 50 | Max-min | Plot the infinities and the ends FIRST; the critical points are the last piece of scaffolding, and a maximum can just as easily sit at an endpoint or a discontinuity as at a place where $f'=0$.
math120.1.10 | MATH 120 | 50 | Related Rates | A max-min word problem is three steps — draw it, name the variables, eliminate one using the constraint — and the critical point is only a candidate until you have checked the ends.
math120.1.11 | MATH 120 | 53 | Newton's Method | Related rates is the chain rule applied to a picture: write the geometric relation, differentiate it with respect to time BEFORE substituting any number, and only then plug in.
math120.1.12 | MATH 120 | 50 | Mean Value Theorem | The Mean Value Theorem upgrades “the difference quotient is APPROXIMATELY the derivative” to “it is EXACTLY the derivative somewhere”, and that single upgrade is what licenses every claim that the sign of $f'$ controls $f$.
math120.1.13 | MATH 120 | 49 | Antiderivatives | Antidifferentiation is every derivative formula read backwards, and the only ambiguity it carries is an additive constant — which the Mean Value Theorem is what guarantees.
math120.1.14 | MATH 120 | 45 | Differential Equations | Separation of variables is the one technique here, and it works whenever $dy/dx$ factors into a function of $x$ times a function of $y$ — Leibniz's notation is what makes the algebra feel legal.
math120.1.15 | MATH 120 | 47 | Definite Integrals | A definite integral is the limit of a sum of rectangle areas, and doing even one by hand — Archimedes' parabola — is what makes the shortcut coming next worth having.
math120.1.16 | MATH 120 | 48 | First Fundamental Theorem | The Fundamental Theorem replaces the whole Riemann-sum apparatus with one subtraction: if $F' = f$ then $\int_{a}^{b}f = F(b)-F(a)$, and yesterday's labour becomes ten seconds.
math120.1.17 | MATH 120 | 50 | Second Fundamental Theorem | Read the Fundamental Theorem backwards and it becomes a machine for MAKING functions: $G(x)=\int_{a}^{x}f(t)\,dt$ always solves $y'=f$ with $y(a)=0$, even when no formula for $G$ exists.
math120.1.18 | MATH 120 | 50 | Applications to Logarithms | Defining $\ln x$ as $\int_{1}^{x}dt/t$ makes every one of its properties a manipulation of integrals — and the same construction hands you functions, like the bell curve's area, that no formula can express.
math120.1.19 | MATH 120 | 50 | Volumes | A volume is a sum of slices, $\int A(x)\,dx$ — and for a solid of revolution the slice is either a disk or a cylindrical shell, decided entirely by which way you cut the two-dimensional picture.
math120.1.20 | MATH 120 | 49 | Work, Probability | An average is an integral divided by the total, a weighted average divides by the total WEIGHT, and probability is the same fraction with the numerator restricted to the part you care about.
math120.1.21 | MATH 120 | 50 | Numerical Integration | Heat, work and energy are one quantity in different units; a probability over a plane is a volume of revolution, not an area; and Simpson's rule is a weighted average clever enough to be worth the extra bookkeeping.
math120.1.22 | MATH 120 | 49 | Exam 3 Review | Exam 3 is five questions — the Fundamental Theorem, the three numerical rules, areas, volumes, and one cumulative sum — and this lecture also settles the $\sqrt{\pi}$ that has been outstanding since the error function appeared.
math120.1.23 | MATH 120 | 47 | Trig Integrals | For $\int\sin^{m}x\cos^{n}x\,dx$ there are exactly two cases: an odd exponent means substitute, all-even means grind the powers away with the half-angle formulas.
math120.1.24 | MATH 120 | 48 | Inverse Substitution | Three square roots, three substitutions: $\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}$ wants $x=a\sin\theta$, $\sqrt{a^{2}+x^{2}}$ wants $a\tan\theta$, $\sqrt{x^{2}-a^{2}}$ wants $a\sec\theta$ — and completing the square turns any quadratic into one of the three.
math120.1.25 | MATH 120 | 49 | Partial Fractions | Any ratio of polynomials can be integrated, because partial fractions splits it back into the simple pieces someone added together — and the cover-up method recovers each coefficient in one line.
math120.1.26 | MATH 120 | 51 | Integration by Parts | Integration by parts is the product rule integrated, and it earns its keep when one factor gets SIMPLER on differentiating while the other gets no worse on integrating.
math120.1.27 | MATH 120 | 45 | Parametric Equations | Arc length is the Pythagorean theorem applied to infinitesimals — $ds = \sqrt{dx^{2}+dy^{2}}$ — and everything else in this lecture is that one element multiplied by something.
math120.1.28 | MATH 120 | 49 | Polar Coordinates | Stop thinking of $y$ as a function of $x$: both are labels for a place, and you may describe that place with whatever coordinate is convenient — a parameter $t$, or a radius and an angle.
math120.1.29 | MATH 120 | 49 | Exam 4 Review | Exam 4 is 55 points of technique — trig substitution, parts, partial fractions — and 45 points of setup: parametric curves, arc length, surfaces of revolution, and polar area, where the only hard part is the limits.
math120.1.30 | MATH 120 | 49 | Indeterminate Forms | L'Hopital's rule replaces $\frac{f}{g}$ by $\frac{f'}{g'}$ — not the quotient rule, just two separate derivatives — but ONLY while the form is still $\frac00$ or $\frac\infty\infty$.
math120.1.31 | MATH 120 | 49 | Improper Integrals | An improper integral is a limit, and the only question is whether the tail's area is finite — $\int_{1}^{\infty}\frac{dx}{x^{p}}$ converges exactly when $p \gt 1$, and that one fact settles most others by comparison.
math120.1.32 | MATH 120 | 50 | Infinite Series | A series is the limit of its partial sums, and the same comparison machinery decides it — with the integral standing in for the sum, because a Riemann sum with $\Delta x = 1$ IS the series.
math120.1.33 | MATH 120 | 48 | Taylor's Series | A power series is a decimal expansion for FUNCTIONS, and Taylor's formula $a_{n} = \frac{f^{(n)}(0)}{n!}$ is how you find the digits.
math120.1.34 | MATH 120 | 39 | Final Review | Power series behave exactly like polynomials inside their radius of convergence — you may multiply, differentiate, integrate and substitute term by term — so one known series generates a dozen more without ever using Taylor's formula again.

### MATH 130 — Harvard Statistics 110 — Joe Blitzstein (full course)
math130.0.0 | MATH 130 | 46 | Probability and Counting | The naive definition — favourable outcomes over possible outcomes — is correct only when the outcomes are equally likely and finite in number, and the rest of this lecture is learning to count the two numbers.
math130.0.1 | MATH 130 | 46 | Story Proofs, Axioms of Probability | A story proof counts the same thing two ways and reads off the identity — and the whole of probability rests on just two axioms once you stop assuming outcomes are equally likely.
math130.0.2 | MATH 130 | 49 | Birthday Problem, Properties of Probability | Twenty-three people suffice for a better-than-even birthday match, because the quantity that matters is not $k$ but the $\binom{k}{2}$ PAIRS — and inclusion-exclusion is the general tool for the probability of a union.
math130.0.3 | MATH 130 | 50 | Conditional Probability | Conditional probability is $P(A\mid B) = \dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$ — restrict the world to $B$ and renormalise — and conditioning is the soul of statistics, because it is how beliefs get updated by evidence.
math130.0.4 | MATH 130 | 50 | Conditioning Continued, Law of Total Probability | Break a hard probability into disjoint cases and add them up — the law of total probability — and pair it with Bayes' rule, because the quantity you want is almost never the one you were given.
math130.0.5 | MATH 130 | 49 | Monty Hall, Simpson's Paradox | Condition on ALL the evidence — in Monty Hall the evidence is not that door 2 has a goat but that Monty opened it — and remember that an inequality holding in every stratum can reverse when the strata are pooled.
math130.0.6 | MATH 130 | 52 | Gambler's Ruin and Random Variables | Condition on the FIRST STEP and a problem with no obvious end becomes a difference equation — and a random variable is not a variable at all but a function from the sample space to the real line.
math130.0.7 | MATH 130 | 50 | Random Variables and Their Distributions | A random variable and its DISTRIBUTION are different objects — the house and the blueprint — and the distribution is carried either by the PMF, which says what each value weighs, or by the CDF, which says how much weight is at or below each point.
math130.0.8 | MATH 130 | 50 | Expectation, Indicator Random Variables, Linearity | The expected value is a weighted average of values by their probabilities — and LINEARITY, $E(X+Y) = E(X) + E(Y)$ whether or not $X$ and $Y$ are independent, is the single most useful fact about it.
math130.0.9 | MATH 130 | 50 | Expectation Continued | Linearity is proved by summing over the SAMPLE SPACE rather than over values — and once you have it, indicators plus symmetry crack problems that defeat the direct approach entirely.
math130.0.10 | MATH 130 | 43 | The Poisson distribution | The Poisson is what you get when a LARGE number of unlikely, weakly dependent things could each happen — and the only number you need is $\lambda$, the expected count.
math130.0.11 | MATH 130 | 50 | Discrete vs. Continuous, the Uniform | In the continuous world the PMF becomes a probability DENSITY, which is not a probability — you integrate it to get one — and every discrete idea has an exact counterpart with a sum replaced by an integral.
math130.0.12 | MATH 130 | 51 | Normal distribution | The standard normal's density is $e^{-z^{2}/2}$ divided by the one constant that makes it integrate to 1 — and that constant, $\sqrt{2\pi}$, comes from an integral nobody can do, solved by writing it down twice.
math130.0.13 | MATH 130 | 49 | Location, Scale, and LOTUS | There is really only ONE normal distribution: every other is $\mu + \sigma Z$, a shift and a stretch of the standard one — and variance, unlike expectation, pulls constants out SQUARED and does not add unless the pieces are independent.
math130.0.14 | MATH 130 | 38 | Midterm Review | A revision sheet, not a new argument: break a hard count into a sum and use linearity, use symmetry before calculus, apply LOTUS to whichever variable has the simple density, and never confuse the distribution, the random variable, and a number.
math130.0.15 | MATH 130 | 18 | Exponential Distribution | The exponential is the continuous waiting time with NO MEMORY: however long you have already waited, the remaining wait is distributed exactly as it was at the start.
math130.0.16 | MATH 130 | 51 | Moment Generating Functions | The moment generating function $M(t) = E(e^{tX})$ is a bookkeeping device that stores every moment in one Taylor series — and it determines the distribution and turns sums of independent variables into products.
math130.0.17 | MATH 130 | 50 | MGFs Continued | Once you have an MGF, read the moments off its Taylor series instead of integrating — and multiply MGFs to find the distribution of a sum, provided the pieces are independent.
math130.0.18 | MATH 130 | 50 | Joint, Conditional, and Marginal Distributions | Joint, conditional, marginal: integrate the joint density to get a marginal, divide the joint by a marginal to get a conditional — and use the two-dimensional LOTUS to take expectations without ever finding a new distribution.
math130.0.19 | MATH 130 | 49 | Multinomial and Cauchy | The multinomial counts objects falling into $k$ categories, and its marginals, lumps and conditionals all come from the story without algebra; the Cauchy, a ratio of two normals, has a density found by differentiating an integral nobody can do.
math130.0.20 | MATH 130 | 49 | Covariance and Correlation | Covariance measures how two variables move together and is what the variance of a sum needs; correlation is covariance after standardising, always between $-1$ and $1$ — and zero correlation does not mean independence.
math130.0.21 | MATH 130 | 48 | Transformations and Convolutions | To find the density of a transformed variable, multiply the old density by $\left|\frac{dx}{dy}\right|$ — the Jacobian in higher dimensions — and to show that something exists, it can be enough to show that a random choice has it with positive probability.
math130.0.22 | MATH 130 | 50 | Beta distribution | The Beta is the flexible family of distributions on $(0,1)$ — a probability for a probability — and it is conjugate to the binomial: start with a Beta prior, observe successes and failures, and the posterior is Beta again with the counts added.
math130.0.23 | MATH 130 | 49 | Gamma distribution and Poisson process | The Gamma function extends the factorial, $\Gamma(n) = (n-1)!$, and the Gamma distribution is the waiting time for the $n$th arrival in a Poisson process — a sum of IID exponentials, as the negative binomial is a sum of geometrics.
math130.0.24 | MATH 130 | 48 | Order Statistics and Conditional Expectation | The bank-and-post-office story ties Gamma to Beta — the total wait is independent of the fraction spent at the bank — which yields the Beta's normalising constant; and the $j$th smallest of $n$ IID uniforms is $\mathrm{Beta}(j, n-j+1)$.
math130.0.25 | MATH 130 | 50 | Conditional Expectation Continued | Conditioning on information does not let you forget it afterwards: that single slip is the whole two-envelope paradox. And $E(Y \mid X)$ is a RANDOM VARIABLE — a function of $X$ — your best prediction of $Y$ once $X$ is known.
math130.0.26 | MATH 130 | 51 | Conditional Expectation given an R.V. | Four properties drive all of conditional expectation — take out what's known, drop the condition under independence, Adam's law $E(E(Y|X)) = E(Y)$, and residuals uncorrelated with any function of $X$ — plus Eve's law, which splits a variance into within-group and between-group parts.
math130.0.27 | MATH 130 | 47 | Inequalities | Four inequalities — Cauchy–Schwarz, Jensen, Markov and Chebyshev — give bounds that are crude but GUARANTEED, and a bound can be defended in a way an approximation cannot.
math130.0.28 | MATH 130 | 50 | Law of Large Numbers and Central Limit Theorem | The law of large numbers says the sample mean converges to the true mean; the central limit theorem says that, scaled by $\sqrt n$, its fluctuations are NORMAL — whatever the distribution you started from.
math130.0.29 | MATH 130 | 47 | Chi-Square, Student-t, Multivariate Normal | The remaining famous distributions are all built from normals: chi-square is a sum of squared normals (a Gamma in disguise), Student-$t$ is a normal over an independent chi-square root, and the multivariate normal is defined by every linear combination being normal.
math130.0.30 | MATH 130 | 47 | Markov Chains | A Markov chain is a random process where the future depends on the past ONLY through the present — and its whole behaviour is carried by one transition matrix, whose powers give the probabilities many steps ahead.
math130.0.31 | MATH 130 | 48 | Markov Chains Continued | For an irreducible finite chain the stationary distribution exists, is unique, and equals one over the mean return time — and for REVERSIBLE chains it can be found with no linear algebra at all: a random walk on an undirected network spends time in proportion to each node's degree.
math130.0.32 | MATH 130 | 47 | Markov Chains Continued Further | Every reversible chain is a random walk on a weighted undirected network, with stationary probability proportional to each node's total weight — and Google's PageRank is a NON-reversible chain whose stationary distribution is computed by simply running it.
math130.0.33 | MATH 130 | 37 | A Look Ahead | A survey, not an argument: the course's ten essential ideas, and where each leads — inference, regression, finance, computational biology, stochastic processes and survey sampling all run on the conditioning, symmetry and expectation developed here.

### AI 200 — Unit I — Primer: But what is a neural network? (3Blue1Brown)

### AI 200 — Unit II — Zero to Hero (Andrej Karpathy)
ai200.1.0 | AI 200 | 146 | Micrograd — spelled-out intro to neural networks and backpropagation | Backpropagation is the chain rule applied node by node over an expression graph: each operation knows only its local derivative, gradients flow from the output back through a topological order, and they ADD wherever a value is used more than once — about a hundred lines of Python, and the same numbers PyTorch gives.
ai200.1.1 | AI 200 | 118 | Makemore 1 — bigram character-level language model | A bigram language model can be built two ways — count which character follows which and normalise, or train a one-layer net with a softmax on the negative log likelihood — and the two arrive at the same model, which is the point: the neural framing is the one that scales.
ai200.1.2 | AI 200 | 76 | Makemore 2 — MLP, following Bengio et al. 2003 | To see more than one character back, stop counting and learn: embed each character as a small vector, concatenate the last three, and feed them through a hidden layer — Bengio et al.'s MLP — trained on minibatches and judged on data it never trained on.
ai200.1.3 | AI 200 | 116 | Makemore 3 — activations, gradients, BatchNorm | A deep net trains well only if its activations and gradients stay well scaled from the first step: start with an output that is unconfident, hidden units that are not saturated, weights scaled by fan-in — and batch normalisation to hold every layer's pre-activations near unit Gaussian — then watch the statistics instead of guessing.
ai200.1.4 | AI 200 | 115 | Makemore 4 — becoming a backprop ninja (DO NOT SKIP) | Backprop is not magic to be trusted but arithmetic to be done: chunk the forward pass into small steps, push the gradient back through each by hand at the level of whole tensors, check every one against PyTorch — then collapse cross-entropy and batch norm into a single analytic backward each.
ai200.1.5 | AI 200 | 56 | Makemore 5 — building a WaveNet | Seeing more context helps, but squashing eight characters into one layer is crude: fuse them a pair at a time — a tree, as in WaveNet — with PyTorch-style modules, and mind the shapes, because one wrong reduction dimension in batch norm silently costs performance.
ai200.1.6 | AI 200 | 116 | Let's build GPT — from scratch, in code | A GPT is a bigram model that learned to look back: tokens gather information from earlier positions through masked, scaled self-attention, compute on it with a feed-forward net, and stack those blocks with residual connections and layer norms — each addition visibly lowering the validation loss on Tiny Shakespeare.
ai200.1.7 | AI 200 | 134 | Let's build the GPT Tokenizer | A tokenizer is a separate model with its own training set and algorithm: byte-level BPE starts from the 256 bytes and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair, encode() replays those merges in the order they were learned, and many of an LLM's weird behaviours trace back to the chunks this produces.
ai200.1.8 | AI 200 | 241 | Let's reproduce GPT-2 (124M) | Reproducing GPT-2 (124M) is the GPT from before plus everything that makes it real: the exact architecture so OpenAI's weights load, GPT-2's initialisation, a long list of speed-ups, GPT-3's optimisation recipe — AdamW, clipping, warmup and cosine decay, a 0.5M-token batch via gradient accumulation — and honest evaluation on held-out loss and HellaSwag.

### AI 210 — fast.ai 2022 — Part 1
ai210.0.0 | AI 210 | 83 | Lesson 1: Getting started | Deep learning is taught here top-down: train a working image classifier in minutes first, then name what happened — Samuel's loop of weights, an automatic measure of performance and an automatic way to improve it — and learn the discipline that keeps it honest: a validation set, and a test set hidden even from yourself.
ai210.0.1 | AI 210 | 77 | Lesson 2: Deployment | A model is only useful once someone can use it: design a project around data you can actually get, train a quick model and let it show you what is wrong with the data, then export it — architecture, weights and data pipeline in one file — and serve it from a plain CPU behind a small web app.
ai210.0.2 | AI 210 | 90 | Lesson 3: Neural net foundations | A neural network is a function that multiplies inputs by parameters, adds them up and replaces negatives with zero, layer after layer — and training is just gradient descent: measure a loss, ask for its gradient, step every parameter a little the other way, repeat. Enough rectified lines added together can fit anything; the rest is making it fast.
ai210.0.3 | AI 210 | 95 | Lesson 4: Natural language (NLP) | A pretrained transformer from the Hugging Face hub can be fine-tuned to almost any text problem once the problem is phrased as text in, label out: build the input string, tokenize and numericalize it, hold out a validation set (and a test set you rarely look at), pick the metric you will be judged on, and train with the largest learning rate that does not break.
ai210.0.4 | AI 210 | 103 | Lesson 5: From-scratch model | Everything a deep learning library does can be written in a page of PyTorch: clean and scale the table, multiply by coefficients, measure a loss, call backward, step and zero the gradients — then swap the sum for matrix products, add a ReLU and a hidden layer, and you have a neural net. Doing it once by hand is what makes the framework's defaults make sense.
ai210.0.5 | AI 210 | 103 | Lesson 6: Random forests | A random forest is nothing but binary splits, stacked into trees, averaged over many trees grown on random subsets — simple enough to build from scratch in a notebook, hard to break, and unusually easy to interpret. Benchmark a one-split model before anything fancier, and remember what a forest cannot do: predict outside the range it was trained on.
ai210.0.6 | AI 210 | 107 | Lesson 7: Collaborative filtering | Bigger models fit in a fixed GPU by accumulating gradients over smaller batches, and an average of several strong models beats any one. Then the lesson turns to recommendations: give every user and every item a few learned numbers — latent factors — predict a rating as their dot product plus biases, and keep the weights small with weight decay. Softmax and cross-entropy, worked in a spreadsheet, are the loss behind classification.
ai210.0.7 | AI 210 | 97 | Lesson 8: Convolutions (CNNs) | An embedding is just an array lookup that behaves, for gradients, like multiplying by a one-hot matrix — and what it learns can be read: biases, directions, distances. A convolution is just a small kernel slid across an image, multiplying and adding; stack stride-2 convolutions with ReLUs, pool, drop out, and finish with a dense layer, and you have a CNN.

### PHYS 100 — MIT 8.01 — Walter Lewin (Fall 1999)
phys100.0.0 | PHYS 100 | 3 | Introduction | What 8.01 is for, in Lewin's words: not to cover a great deal but to UNCOVER a few basic things you will remember for the rest of your life — and to make you see the beauty of physics.
phys100.0.1 | PHYS 100 | 38 | Units, Dimensions, and Scaling Arguments | Every quantity in mechanics is built from length, time and mass — and dimensional analysis alone can tell you HOW an answer scales, provided you choose the right variables and never forget that a measurement without its uncertainty is meaningless.
phys100.0.2 | PHYS 100 | 51 | Introduction to Kinematics | Velocity is $dx/dt$ and acceleration is $dv/dt = d^{2}x/dt^{2}$ — two equations to remember for the rest of your life — and signs matter: they depend on which direction you call positive, not on where you put zero.
phys100.0.3 | PHYS 100 | 50 | Vectors | Vectors add head to tail and decompose into perpendicular components — and that decomposition turns a complicated motion in three dimensions into three independent one-dimensional motions.
phys100.0.4 | PHYS 100 | 52 | The Motion of Projectiles | A projectile is a constant-velocity motion sideways and a constant-acceleration motion vertically, and from those two alone come the parabola, the maximum height, the range $v_0^{2}\sin2\alpha/g$ — and the monkey that cannot escape.
phys100.0.5 | PHYS 100 | 51 | Uniform Circular Motion | Going round a circle at constant speed still means accelerating — toward the centre, with magnitude $v^{2}/r = \omega^{2}r$ — and something must push or pull to supply it; remove that push and the object flies off along the tangent, not in a spiral.
phys100.0.6 | PHYS 100 | 49 | Newton's First, Second, and Third Laws | Newton's three laws: without a net force velocity stays constant; $\vec F = m\vec a$ defines force; and every force comes with an equal and opposite force on the other body — none provable, all believed because every measurement agrees with them.
phys100.0.7 | PHYS 100 | 50 | Weight, Perceived Gravity, and Weightlessnes | Your WEIGHT is the push or pull that supports you — what a bathroom scale reads — not the gravitational force $mg$. Accelerate up and you weigh more; accelerate down and you weigh less; fall freely and you weigh nothing, though gravity has not changed at all.
phys100.0.8 | PHYS 100 | 48 | Frictional Forces | Friction grows to match whatever push it must resist, up to a maximum $\mu N$ — and that maximum is, surprisingly, independent of the mass and of the contact area; only the pair of materials matters.
phys100.0.9 | PHYS 100 | 50 | Review of Lectures 1 through 5 | A revision sheet for the first exam: scaling, vectors, one-dimensional motion read off a graph, projectiles as two independent motions, and uniform circular motion — each worked with numbers.
phys100.0.10 | PHYS 100 | 49 | Hooke's Law, Simple Harmonic Oscillator | A force that pulls back in proportion to the displacement, $F = -kx$, gives simple harmonic motion: $x = A\cos(\omega t + \varphi)$ with $\omega = \sqrt{k/m}$ — and a period that does not depend on how far you pull it.
phys100.0.11 | PHYS 100 | 49 | Work, Energy, and Universal Gravitation | Work is force times displacement, $W = \int \vec F \cdot d\vec r$, and it equals the change in kinetic energy. For a conservative force like gravity the work depends only on the endpoints, so mechanical energy $K + U$ is conserved.
phys100.0.12 | PHYS 100 | 50 | Resistive Forces | Drag on a sphere has two parts, $F = C_1 r v + C_2 r^{2} v^{2}$: viscous at low speed, pressure at high speed. When drag equals weight the object stops accelerating, and that terminal speed scales as $r^{2}$ in the first regime and $\sqrt r$ in the second.
phys100.0.13 | PHYS 100 | 52 | Equation of Motion for Simple Harmonic Oscillators | Force is minus the slope of the potential, $F = -dU/dx$. Near any minimum of $U$ the potential is a parabola, so small motions about a stable equilibrium are simple harmonic — and energy conservation gives the period without drawing a single force.
phys100.0.14 | PHYS 100 | 50 | Orbits and Escape Velocity | To escape the Earth, total energy must reach zero: $v_{esc} = \sqrt{2GM/R}$, about 11.2 km/s. A circular orbit needs $\sqrt{GM/r}$, exactly $\sqrt2$ less. Then power, $P = \vec F \cdot \vec v$, and how little of our energy use is muscle.
phys100.0.15 | PHYS 100 | 53 | Momentum and Its Conservation | Momentum $\vec p = m\vec v$ obeys $d\vec p_{tot}/dt = \vec F_{ext}$: the internal forces cancel in pairs, so with no net external force the total momentum cannot change — however much kinetic energy is destroyed, and however wildly the parts move.
phys100.0.16 | PHYS 100 | 49 | Elastic and Inelastic Collisions | Momentum gives one equation; for a second you need to know what happens to the kinetic energy. In an elastic collision none is lost — and in the centre-of-mass frame each object simply bounces back with its speed unchanged.
phys100.0.17 | PHYS 100 | 49 | Momentum of Individual Objects, Rocket Equation | An impulse $\int F\,dt$ is a change of momentum. That idea measures a bullet's speed with a pendulum, puts forces of hundreds of newtons into a bouncing ball, and — as a steady stream of expelled mass — drives a rocket: $\Delta v = -u\ln(m_f/m_i) - gt$.
phys100.0.18 | PHYS 100 | 50 | Review of Lectures 6 through 15 | A revision sheet for the second exam: the work-energy theorem (always) against conservation of mechanical energy (conservative forces only), then the pendulum and the spring, orbital energy, drag in syrup, and a completely inelastic collision.
phys100.0.19 | PHYS 100 | 41 | Rotating Rigid Bodies, Inertia, and Axis Theorems | A rotating body stores kinetic energy $\tfrac12I\omega^{2}$, where $I = \sum m_ir_i^{2}$ depends on the shape AND the axis. The parallel- and perpendicular-axis theorems extend a table of moments of inertia — and put numbers on flywheels, the Earth and a pulsar.
phys100.0.20 | PHYS 100 | 51 | Angular Momentum | Angular momentum $\vec L = \vec r \times \vec p$ depends on the point you measure from; torque $\vec\tau = \vec r \times \vec F$ changes it. With no net external torque it is conserved — which is why a skater spins up, and why a collapsing star becomes a millisecond pulsar.
phys100.0.21 | PHYS 100 | 48 | Torque | Choose the origin that makes the torque easy: about a fixed pivot, forces at the pivot drop out. That turns a swinging ruler or a hula hoop into $\tau = I\alpha$, a simple harmonic oscillator, and a period you can predict to half a percent.
phys100.0.22 | PHYS 100 | 49 | Kepler's Laws, Elliptical Orbits, and Maneuvers | Bound orbits are ellipses, and their energy and period depend only on the semimajor axis: $E = -GMm/2a$, $T^{2} = 4\pi^{2}a^{3}/GM$. Energy fixes $a$; angular momentum about the central body fixes where perigee and apogee are.
phys100.0.23 | PHYS 100 | 50 | Doppler Effect, Binary Stars, Neutron Stars, Black Holes | Motion toward or away from you shifts frequency: $\lambda'/\lambda = 1 - (v/c)\cos\theta$. In binary stars the shifting spectral lines give orbital speeds, radii and periods — then, through Kepler's third law, masses, and the evidence for neutron stars and black holes.
phys100.0.24 | PHYS 100 | 50 | Rolling Motion, Gyroscopes | A rolling object's acceleration down a slope, $a = \dfrac{g\sin\beta}{1 + I/MR^{2}}$, depends only on its shape. And torque on a spinning wheel does not tip it over: the spin angular momentum chases the torque, and the wheel precesses.
phys100.0.25 | PHYS 100 | 48 | Static Equilibrium, Stability, Rope Walker | Static equilibrium needs BOTH the net force and the net torque to be zero. That decides when a ladder slips, how a few turns of rope around a post hold a huge load, and why anything hanging freely settles with its centre of mass below the pivot.
phys100.0.26 | PHYS 100 | 50 | Elasticity and Young's Modulus | A rod stretches like a spring: $F/A = Y\,\Delta\ell/\ell$, stress equals Young's modulus times strain. Past the elastic limit it deforms for good, flows, and breaks — and Young's modulus also sets the speed of sound, $v = \sqrt{Y/\rho}$.
phys100.0.27 | PHYS 100 | 50 | Gases and Incompressible Liquids | Pressure in a fluid is transmitted undiminished (Pascal), and gravity adds $\rho g h$ with depth. We live under an ocean of air pressing at about $10^{5}$ Pa — enough to crush a can and hold a 10 m column of water — and our lungs can fight only a tenth of it.
phys100.0.28 | PHYS 100 | 49 | Hydrostatics, Archimedes' Principle, Fluid Dynamics | A body in a fluid is pushed up by the weight of the fluid it displaces (Archimedes). That decides floating and sinking, gives densities without cutting anything, and explains stability. Moving fluids trade pressure for speed: $\tfrac12\rho v^{2} + \rho gy + P$ is constant (Bernoulli).
phys100.0.29 | PHYS 100 | 50 | Review of Lectures 16 through 24 | A revision sheet for the third exam: collisions, the Atwood machine with a massive pulley, the physical pendulum, an elliptical orbit from its launch, Doppler shift, and a ball rolling down a slope — each set up the same way, with forces, torques and the conservation laws.
phys100.0.30 | PHYS 100 | 50 | Simple Harmonic Oscillations of Suspended Solid Bodies | Any body swinging about a pivot has $T = 2\pi\sqrt{I_P/Mgb}$. A rod, a ring, a disk and a simple pendulum can all be built to beat in time. The same energy method gives the period of liquid sloshing in a U-tube, and a torsion pendulum is a spring for angles.
phys100.0.31 | PHYS 100 | 48 | Pendulums and Springs | Drive an oscillator at a frequency of your choosing and, once the transient dies, it follows you with amplitude $\dfrac{F_0/m}{\omega_0^{2} - \omega^{2}}$. Near its natural frequency the response explodes — resonance, the physics of violins, organ pipes, shattered wineglasses and the Tacoma Narrows Bridge.
phys100.0.32 | PHYS 100 | 49 | Thermal Expansion | Heat most things and they grow: $\Delta L = \alpha L\,\Delta T$, and for volume $\beta = 3\alpha$. Small as the numbers are, they bend bimetal strips into thermostats, drive mercury up a thermometer — and water, alone, shrinks as it warms from 0 to 4 °C.
phys100.0.33 | PHYS 100 | 53 | Ideal-Gas Law | For a gas, $PV = nRT$ — and the mass of the molecules does not appear. So at one temperature every gas has the same $mv^{2}$, a mole of anything fills 24 litres at room conditions, and an isothermal atmosphere thins as $e^{-h/8\,\text{km}}$.
phys100.0.34 | PHYS 100 | 48 | Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle | On the scale of atoms, classical physics fails: electrons sit only in discrete energy levels, light and matter are both waves and particles ($\lambda = h/p$), and position and momentum cannot both be sharp — $\Delta p\,\Delta x \gtrsim \hbar$.
phys100.0.35 | PHYS 100 | 44 | Professor Lewin’s Early days at MIT | Lewin's own research story: how x-ray astronomy began, why he flew telescopes on enormous balloons to the top of the atmosphere, and how x-ray binaries — and thermonuclear bursts on neutron stars — came to be understood.
phys100.0.36 | PHYS 100 | 61 | For the Love of Physics (Walter Lewin's Last Lecture) | Lewin's last lecture, 'For the Love of Physics': the course in miniature — a pendulum whose period ignores amplitude and mass, a wrecking ball that stops at his chin, the blue sky and the red sunset made in a bucket — and his one piece of advice: you have to love it.

### MATH 210 — Unit I — Matrix Calculus (MIT 18.S096, Edelman & Johnson)
math210.0.0 | MATH 210 | 58 | Lecture 1 Part 1: Introduction and Motivation | Calculus should run scalar → vector → matrix, and a derivative is best seen as a LINEARIZATION: $df = f'(x)\,dx$, with $f'(x)$ a linear operator acting on the small change. For matrices this is not a trivial generalisation — $d(X^{2}) = X\,dX + dX\,X$, not $2X\,dX$.
math210.0.1 | MATH 210 | 48 | Lecture 1 Part 2: Derivatives as Linear Operators | Johnson's precise version: the derivative is the linear operator $f'(x)$ with $f(x + \delta x) - f(x) = f'(x)\,\delta x + o(\delta x)$. Linear operators live on any vector space, so this definition works for vectors, matrices and even functions — and for a scalar of a vector it DEFINES the gradient, $df = \nabla f \cdot dx$.
math210.0.2 | MATH 210 | 74 | Lecture 2 Part 1: Derivatives in Higher Dimensions: Jacobians and Matrix Functions | A nonlinear map is locally linear, and its Jacobian is that local linear map. The sum, product and chain rules all carry over — keeping order. And the order you multiply the chain rule's Jacobians is not a detail: right-to-left is forward mode, left-to-right is reverse mode, and for one output and many inputs reverse mode wins by a factor of $n$.
math210.0.3 | MATH 210 | 30 | Lecture 2 Part 2: Vectorization of Matrix Functions | Inputs and outputs can themselves be matrices. The product rule gives $d(A^{3}) = dA\,A^{2} + A\,dA\,A + A^{2}dA$ — which cannot be simplified — and differentiating $A^{-1}A = I$ gives $d(A^{-1}) = -A^{-1}\,dA\,A^{-1}$, the matrix version of $-dA/A^{2}$.
math210.0.4 | MATH 210 | 53 | Lecture 3 Part 1: Kronecker Products and Jacobians | The Kronecker product lets you write a matrix-to-matrix derivative as an explicit Jacobian without ever forming it: $(A \otimes B)\,\mathrm{vec}(C) = \mathrm{vec}(BCA^{T})$. With it, $d(X^{2}) = (I \otimes X + X^{T} \otimes I)\,\mathrm{vec}(dX)$ — and matrix factorizations such as LU and eigendecompositions become functions with Jacobians too.
math210.0.5 | MATH 210 | 51 | Lecture 3 Part 2: Finite-Difference Approximations | Finite differences are a poor way to compute derivatives but the best way to CHECK them. The error of $f(x + \delta x) - f(x)$ against $f'(x)\,\delta x$ falls linearly with $\delta x$ (truncation) until floating-point roundoff takes over; a step near $\sqrt{\varepsilon} \approx 10^{-8}$ times $x$ balances the two.
math210.0.6 | MATH 210 | 64 | Lecture 4 Part 1: Gradients and Inner Products in Other Vector Spaces | A gradient needs an inner product. Pick one on your vector space — for matrices, the Frobenius product $A \cdot B = \mathrm{tr}(A^{T}B)$ — and the gradient of any scalar function is whatever you dot with $dA$ to get $df$. So $\nabla\|A\|_F = A/\|A\|_F$ and $\nabla_A(x^{T}Ay) = xy^{T}$.
math210.0.7 | MATH 210 | 44 | Lecture 4 Part 2: Nonlinear Root Finding, Optimization, and Adjoint Gradient Methods | Derivatives drive Newton's method (linearize, solve, repeat) and optimisation (go downhill along $-\nabla f$). When $f$ depends on parameters through the solution of $Ax = b$ or $g(x, p) = 0$, the adjoint method gets the whole gradient for ONE extra solve with the transposed system — reverse mode, backpropagation, by another name.
math210.0.8 | MATH 210 | 28 | Lecture 5 Part 1: Derivative of Matrix Determinant and Inverse | A derivative needs a NORM (to say what 'small' means), which is why the setting is a Banach space. The gradient of the determinant is the cofactor matrix, $\nabla\det A = \det(A)\,A^{-T}$, so $d\det A = \det A\,\mathrm{tr}(A^{-1}dA)$ and $d\log\det A = \mathrm{tr}(A^{-1}dA)$.
math210.0.9 | MATH 210 | 36 | Lecture 5 Part 2: Forward Automatic Differentiation via Dual Numbers | Forward-mode automatic differentiation is neither symbolic nor finite differences. Carry a pair — value and derivative — through every operation, with the sum and quotient rules taught to the arithmetic, and an unmodified program returns its exact derivative. Written $a + b\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon^{2} = 0$, these are dual numbers.
math210.0.10 | MATH 210 | 33 | Lecture 5 Part 3: Differentiation on Computational Graphs | Draw a program as a directed acyclic graph with each edge labelled by its one-step derivative. The derivative of an output with respect to an input is the SUM over paths of the PRODUCT of edge labels. Accumulate those path products from the inputs and you have forward mode; from the output, reverse mode.
math210.0.11 | MATH 210 | 58 | Lecture 6 Part 1: Adjoint Differentiation of ODE Solutions | To differentiate the solution of an ODE with respect to many parameters, add a Lagrange multiplier $\lambda(t)$, integrate by parts, and choose $\lambda$ to kill the unknown sensitivities. $\lambda$ solves a linear adjoint ODE BACKWARDS in time, and the gradient becomes an integral — one forward solve, one backward solve, however many parameters.
math210.0.12 | MATH 210 | 43 | Lecture 6 Part 2: Calculus of Variations and Gradients of Functionals | Functions are vectors too, so a functional $f(u) = \int F(u, u', x)\,dx$ has a derivative defined exactly as before: linearize $f(u + du) - f(u)$. With the inner product $\langle u, v\rangle = \int uv\,dx$ and one integration by parts, the gradient is $F_u - (F_{u'})'$. Setting it to zero gives the Euler–Lagrange equation.
math210.0.13 | MATH 210 | 66 | Lecture 7 Part 1: Derivatives of Random Functions | A random function $X(p)$ returns a random variable. Differencing samples taken independently does not work, because the difference never shrinks. The useful derivative comes from samples that SHARE their randomness: write $X(p) = x(p, \omega)$ with $\omega$ drawn from a fixed distribution, and differentiate at fixed $\omega$. This is the reparameterization trick, and its average is $\frac{d}{dp}E[X(p)]$, until the function jumps, as discrete ones do.
math210.0.14 | MATH 210 | 46 | Lecture 7 Part 2: Second Derivatives, Bilinear Forms, and Hessian Matrices | The second derivative is the derivative of the derivative: $f''(x)[dx', dx] = f'(x + dx')[dx] - f'(x)[dx]$. It takes TWO small changes and is linear in each (a bilinear form), and it is always symmetric. For $f: \mathbb{R}^{n} \to \mathbb{R}$ it is $dx'^{T}H\,dx$, with $H$ the symmetric Hessian. Its job is the quadratic approximation behind Newton's method.
math210.0.15 | MATH 210 | 37 | Lecture 8 Part 1: Derivatives of Eigenproblems | Constrained quantities have constrained perturbations: on the sphere $x^{T}dx = 0$, and for an orthogonal $Q$, $Q^{T}dQ$ is antisymmetric. Differentiate $S = Q\Lambda Q^{T}$ and take the diagonal: that gives the Hellmann–Feynman result $d\lambda_i = q_i^{T}\,dS\,q_i$. The off-diagonal entries give the eigenvectors, and break down when eigenvalues collide.
math210.0.16 | MATH 210 | 65 | Lecture 8 Part 2: Automatic Differentiation on Computational Graphs | A program is a directed acyclic graph with one-step partial derivatives on its edges, and every derivative is the sum over paths of the product of edge weights. Forward mode accumulates those products from the inputs and needs no stored graph. Reverse mode records the graph on a forward pass, then accumulates backwards from the output, sharing work along the way. Its cost scales with the number of outputs, which is why machine learning, with a single loss, uses it.

### MATH 210 — Unit II — Optimization for Deep Learning
math210.1.0 | MATH 210 | 75 | Loss functions and optimization (CS231n Lecture 3) | Training a linear classifier needs two things. The first is a LOSS that scores how bad a weight matrix $W$ is: the multiclass SVM's hinge loss or softmax's $-\log$ probability, plus a regularization penalty that prefers simpler $W$. The second is OPTIMIZATION to find a good $W$: follow the negative gradient, computed analytically, checked numerically, and estimated on minibatches.
math210.1.1 | MATH 210 | 80 | Training neural networks I — init, activations, BatchNorm (CS231n Lecture 6) | Four choices decide whether a network can train at all. Use ReLU, not sigmoid. Zero-centre the data. Scale the initial weights by the fan-in (Xavier, with a factor of 2 for ReLU). Add batch normalization. Then babysit the run: check the initial loss, overfit a tiny subset, set the learning rate first, and search hyperparameters at random, on a log scale, from coarse to fine.
math210.1.2 | MATH 210 | 76 | Training neural networks II — momentum, Adam, schedules (CS231n Lecture 7) | Plain SGD zigzags across badly conditioned valleys, crawls near saddle points, and wanders with noisy gradients. Momentum adds velocity. AdaGrad and RMSProp divide each coordinate's step by a running size of its gradient. Adam does both, with bias correction, and is the default. Optimizers reduce TRAINING error; regularization (dropout, data augmentation, batch norm), ensembles and transfer learning close the gap to test error.
math210.1.3 | MATH 210 | 0 | Why momentum really works — read and play with every widget | On a quadratic, gradient descent splits into independent eigen-directions, each shrinking by $|1 - \alpha\lambda_i|$, so the condition number $\kappa = \lambda_n/\lambda_1$ sets the pace: at best $(\kappa - 1)/(\kappa + 1)$ per step. Momentum turns each direction into a damped oscillator, and with the right $\alpha$ and $\beta$ the rate becomes $(\sqrt\kappa - 1)/(\sqrt\kappa + 1)$. That is a square-root speedup, and no first-order method can beat it.
math210.1.4 | MATH 210 | 0 | An overview of gradient descent optimization algorithms (Ruder) | A field guide to the update rules. Gradient descent comes in batch, stochastic and mini-batch variants. Momentum and Nesterov add velocity. Adagrad, Adadelta, RMSprop, Adam, AdaMax and Nadam adapt the learning rate for each parameter. Around them sit practical tricks: shuffling, curriculum learning, batch normalization, early stopping and gradient noise. Adaptive methods suit sparse data; Adam is a sound default; well-tuned SGD with a schedule remains competitive.
math210.1.5 | MATH 210 | 0 | Convexity — Boyd & Vandenberghe ch. 2–3 (free book) | A set is convex if it contains every segment between its points. A function is convex if its graph lies below every chord, or equivalently above every tangent plane, which is why a zero gradient means a GLOBAL minimum. Rather than checking the definition every time, build convex things from known examples using operations that preserve convexity.

### MATH 210 — Unit III — Information Theory (David MacKay, Cambridge)
math210.2.0 | MATH 210 | 62 | Introduction to Information Theory | Shannon's problem is reliable communication over an unreliable channel. Instead of buying better physics, wrap the channel in an encoder that adds redundancy and a decoder that uses inference to remove the noise. Repetition codes lower the error only by driving the rate toward zero. Shannon proved that below the channel's capacity (0.53 for a binary symmetric channel that flips 10% of bits), the error can be made as small as you like at a fixed rate.
math210.2.1 | MATH 210 | 51 | Entropy and Data Compression (I): Introduction to Compression, Inf.Theory and Entropy | Real sources are redundant, so compress first (source coding), then add the right redundancy for the channel. Shannon measures the information in an outcome as $\log_2(1/p)$ bits: zero for a certainty, large for a surprise, and additive for independent events. Its average, the entropy $H(X) = \sum p\log_2(1/p)$, measures a whole ensemble. It turns the weighing puzzle into a recipe: choose the weighing whose outcome has maximum entropy.
math210.2.2 | MATH 210 | 51 | Entropy and Data Compression (II): Shannon's Source Coding Theorem, The Bent Coin Lottery | Three games support Shannon's measure. In 63, six yes/no questions, each worth one bit, identify a number from 0 to 63. In submarine, the information contents of every miss and the final hit always add up to $\log_2 64 = 6$ bits. In the bent-coin lottery, the tickets needed for a 99% chance of winning number about $2^{NH}$. That is the source coding theorem: N outcomes compress to about $NH$ bits.
math210.2.3 | MATH 210 | 57 | Entropy and Data Compression (III): Shannon's Source Coding Theorem, Symbol Codes | A symbol code gives each symbol a binary codeword and concatenates them without punctuation. To be uniquely decodable, its codeword lengths must satisfy the Kraft inequality $\sum 2^{-l_i} \le 1$, a fixed budget: shortening one codeword forces others to lengthen. The expected length is then at least the entropy, reaching it exactly when $l_i = \log_2(1/p_i)$. Prefix codes are easy to decode, and the Huffman algorithm builds an optimal one, always within one bit of $H$.
math210.2.4 | MATH 210 | 63 | Entropy and Data Compression (IV): Shannon's Source Coding Theorem, Symbol Codes | Symbol codes spend at least one bit per symbol, which is hopeless when the next symbol is almost certain, and in English it often is. Arithmetic coding treats the whole file as one interval of $[0, 1)$ of width $P(\text{file})$, subdivided using whatever context-dependent, adaptive probabilities a model supplies. It sends a binary string whose interval fits inside that one, within 2 bits of $\log_2(1/P(\text{file}))$ for the entire file. It cleanly separates modelling from coding.
math210.2.5 | MATH 210 | 55 | Noisy Channel Coding (I): Inference and Information Measures for Noisy Channels | A code whose lengths match the information contents produces output that looks like fair coin flips, so information theory can settle questions without calculation. For noisy channels, inference needs the probability of everything. A channel supplies only $P(y \mid x)$; an input distribution completes the joint. A joint ensemble then gives the entropies $H(X)$, $H(Y)$ and $H(X, Y)$, the conditional entropy $H(X \mid Y) \le H(X)$, and the mutual information $I(X; Y) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y)$: the overlap that measures how much the output tells you about the input.
math210.2.6 | MATH 210 | 47 | Noisy Channel Coding (II): The Capacity of a Noisy Channel | A channel is a set of conditional distributions $Q_{j|i} = P(y = b_j \mid x = a_i)$. Choose an input distribution and you have a joint ensemble: Bayes' theorem gives the posterior on the input, and $I(X; Y)$ measures what the output conveys. The capacity is the maximum of $I(X; Y)$ over input distributions. For the binary symmetric channel it is $1 - H_2(f)$, reached with a uniform input.
math210.2.7 | MATH 210 | 69 | Noisy Channel Coding (III): The Noisy-Channel Coding Theorem | The capacity is the rate of virtually error-free communication. N uses of any channel look like a noisy typewriter: each input's typical outputs form a blob of about $2^{NH(Y|X)}$ strings inside $2^{NH(Y)}$, so about $2^{NI(X;Y)}$ inputs can be kept apart. For the binary symmetric channel, averaging the error of a syndrome decoder over all random parity-check matrices shows it vanishes whenever $K/N \lt 1 - H_2(f)$. Almost every code is good, though the proof names none.
math210.2.8 | MATH 210 | 49 | A Noisy Channel Coding Gem, And An Introduction To Bayesian Inference (I) | The binary erasure channel has capacity $1 - f$. A sender who hears every erasure and simply retransmits achieves exactly the same $1 - f$: feedback makes coding easy, but not faster. Then inference. To learn $\mu$ and $\sigma$ of a Gaussian, weigh every hypothesis in the $(\mu, \sigma)$ plane by the density it gave to the data actually seen. The calculator's $\bar x$ and $\sigma_N$ buttons find the peak of that likelihood, and $\sigma_{N-1}$ finds the peak of the marginal likelihood once $\mu$ is integrated out.
math210.2.9 | MATH 210 | 76 | An Introduction To Bayesian Inference (II): Inference Of Parameters And Models | Inferring parameters and comparing models are the same move at two levels. For decays seen only between 1 and 20 cm, the likelihood of a decay length $\lambda$ is $\prod_n e^{-x_n/\lambda}/(\lambda Z(\lambda))$, with $Z(\lambda) = e^{-1/\lambda} - e^{-20/\lambda}$. Write it down, multiply by a prior, and the posterior is the complete answer. To compare models, use the normalizing constant, the evidence $P(D \mid \mathcal H)$, which automatically penalizes models that spread their predictions thin: Occam's razor.
math210.2.10 | MATH 210 | 57 | Approximating Probability Distributions (I):  Clustering As An Example Inference Problem | Clustering is inference in disguise. A channel whose output is Gaussian around one of two means gives a posterior that is a sigmoid of a linear function of $y$. K-means assigns each point to its nearest mean and moves each mean to the average of its points: a hard fit of K equal, spherical, equally weighted Gaussians, so it fails exactly where those assumptions fail. Soft k-means replaces the hard assignment with responsibilities $\propto e^{-\beta d}$. Version 2 also learns each cluster's variances and weight: the EM algorithm for a mixture of Gaussians.
math210.2.11 | MATH 210 | 84 | Approximating Probability Distributions (II): Monte Carlo Methods (I) | Monte Carlo methods answer questions about a distribution you can evaluate only up to a constant, $P(x) = P^*(x)/Z$, by drawing samples. The estimate $\hat\Phi = \frac1R\sum_r \phi(x^{(r)})$ has an error that falls like $\sigma/\sqrt R$, whatever the dimension. The hard part is getting the samples. Uniform, importance and rejection sampling all break down in high dimensions. Metropolis and Gibbs sampling, which wander by local moves, work, but they move like random walks, slowly.
math210.2.12 | MATH 210 | 108 | Approximating Probability Distributions (III): Monte Carlo Methods (II): Slice Sampling | Slice sampling is a Markov chain method with no step size to tune. Draw a height $u$ uniformly under $P^*(x)$, then draw $x$ uniformly from the 'slice' where $P^*(x) \gt u$, found by stepping an interval out and shrinking it on rejections. The theme is suppressing random-walk behaviour, which Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and overrelaxation do too. Ising models show sampling at work: their Gibbs update is a coin toss with a sigmoid bias, and in two dimensions they have a genuine phase transition.
math210.2.13 | MATH 210 | 47 | Approximating Probability Distributions (IV): Variational Methods | Variational methods replace sampling with optimization. Choose a simple, adjustable $Q(x; \theta)$ and minimize the variational free energy $\tilde F(\theta) = \langle E(x)\rangle_Q - H_Q$. That equals $D_{KL}(Q\,\|\,P) - \ln Z$, so minimizing it pulls $Q$ toward $P$ and gives the bound $\tilde F \ge -\ln Z$. $D_{KL}(Q\,\|\,P)$ is the computable direction, and it makes $Q$ avoid places where $P$ is small. For a spin system with separable $Q$, the optimum obeys the mean-field equations $a_m = \beta(\sum_n J_{mn}\bar x_n + h_m)$, $\bar x_m = \tanh a_m$.
math210.2.14 | MATH 210 | 87 | Data Modelling With Neural Networks (I): Feedforward Networks: The Capacity Of A Neuron | Brains do things computers still struggle with: content-addressable memory, and pigeons memorizing arbitrary labels on 725 images for a year. They manage it with raw throughput comparable to a supercomputer, but in a different style: parallel, highly connected, distributed and robust. A neuron computes $a = \sum_k w_kx_k + w_0$ and outputs $f(a)$. Learning means minimizing an objective, here the information content of the labels, whose gradient $-\sum_n(t_n - y_n)x_n$ is all 'backpropagation' means. Weight decay stops the weights blowing up, and a neuron with $K$ inputs can store about $2K$ random labels: 2 bits per weight.
math210.2.15 | MATH 210 | 97 | Data Modelling With Neural Networks (II): Content-Addressable Memories And State | Hopfield's answer to the content-addressable memory challenge is a feedback network with symmetric weights: $a_i = \sum_j w_{ij}x_j + \theta_i$, $x_i = \mathrm{sign}(a_i)$ or $\tanh(a_i)$, trained by Hebb's rule $w_{ij} = \sum_n x_i^{(n)}x_j^{(n)}$. The stored patterns become attracting fixed points: they clean up noise, survive the deletion of half the weights, and a new memory is added by nudging every weight by ±1, until capacity runs out. Spurious states come free. And recall by nearest memory is exactly decoding an error-correcting code.
