### SYS 250 — Unit I — Deep Learning Systems (CMU 10-714, Chen & Kolter)
sys250.0.0 | SYS 250 | 58 | Introduction and Logistics | Deep learning took off less because of any one model than because of easy automatic-differentiation libraries: a ConvNet that once took 44,000 lines and six months now takes about 100 lines and an afternoon. The core ideas underneath are few (automatic differentiation, gradient-based optimization, and fast linear algebra on GPUs), so you can build a capable framework, needle, in about 2,000 lines. Knowing how it works inside makes you faster with the real ones.
sys250.0.1 | SYS 250 | 80 | ML Refresher / Softmax Regression | Every machine-learning algorithm is three choices: a hypothesis class, a loss, and an optimizer. Softmax regression picks a linear map $h_\theta(x) = \theta^{T}x$ to $k$ logits, the cross-entropy loss $-h_y + \log\sum_j e^{h_j}$, and minibatch SGD. Its gradient, found by pretending everything is a scalar and then fixing the shapes, is $\nabla_\theta = \frac1B X^{T}(Z - I_y)$, where $Z$ is the row-wise softmax. That is a few lines of code and under 8% error on MNIST.
sys250.0.2 | SYS 250 | 54 | "Manual" Neural Networks | A linear classifier can only carve space into linear regions. The fix is a feature map, $h = \theta^{T}\phi(x)$, but a linear $\phi$ collapses back into a linear model, so add a nonlinearity: $\phi(x) = \sigma(W^{T}x)$. Training $W$ too makes a two-layer neural network. A neural network is just composed, differentiable, parameterized functions. A two-layer network is a universal approximator, but so are splines; depth is used because, empirically, it works better per parameter.
sys250.0.3 | SYS 250 | 48 | "Manual" Neural Networks | Backpropagation is the chain rule plus caching. For an MLP, $Z_{i+1} = \sigma(Z_iW_i)$, define $G_i = \nabla_{Z_i}\ell$. Then $G_i = (G_{i+1} \circ \sigma'(Z_iW_i))W_i^{T}$ and $\nabla_{W_i}\ell = Z_i^{T}(G_{i+1} \circ \sigma'(Z_iW_i))$: a forward pass stores the $Z_i$, and a backward pass computes the $G_i$. Each layer only has to multiply the incoming gradient by its own derivative (a vector–Jacobian product), which is the modular idea behind automatic differentiation.
sys250.0.4 | SYS 250 | 64 | Automatic Differentiation | Three ways to get gradients. Numerical differences are exact in principle but cost $2n$ evaluations and lose precision, so use them only to CHECK gradients. Symbolic differentiation repeats work. Automatic differentiation walks the computational graph. Forward mode costs one pass per input; reverse mode computes adjoints $\bar v_i = \partial y/\partial v_i$ from the output back, summing over every path, and gets all input gradients in one pass. Modern frameworks do reverse mode by BUILDING a new graph for the gradient, which gives gradients of gradients for free.
sys250.0.5 | SYS 250 | 66 | Automatic Differentiation Implementation | Needle's tensors are nodes of a computational graph. A Value carries cached_data (the array), op (what produced it), inputs (from what), and requires_grad. Each Op defines compute (arrays in, array out) and gradient (Tensors in, Tensors out), so gradients are graphs too. Operator overloading builds the graph. Eager mode computes immediately, lazy mode on demand. And because a tensor remembers its history, accumulating a loss across iterations keeps the whole history alive unless you detach it.
sys250.0.6 | SYS 250 | 87 | Fully connected networks, optimization, initialization | With automatic differentiation, a fully connected network is fully defined by its forward pass: $Z_{i+1} = \sigma_i(Z_iW_i + 1b_i^T)$. What remains is making it train. Plain gradient descent is sensitive to its step size; momentum and Adam smooth and rescale the steps; and initialization matters far more than it looks, because the weights barely move from where they start. For ReLU networks, variance $2/n$ keeps activations the same size layer after layer.
sys250.0.7 | SYS 250 | 60 | Neural Network Abstractions | Deep learning frameworks went through three styles of programming abstraction. Caffe's layers each hand-wrote forward and backward. TensorFlow 1.0 declared a static graph and then ran it in a session, which is good for optimization. PyTorch and needle run imperatively (define-by-run), which is good for debugging and dynamic models. On top of the tensor-level autodiff sit modular components: nn.Module, loss functions, optimizers, initialization and data loaders, each swappable on its own.
sys250.0.8 | SYS 250 | 56 | Neural Network Library Implementation | Building the library in code: the parameter update must go through .data so it does not grow the graph, and softmax must subtract the maximum so it does not overflow. Parameter is a Tensor subclass. Module finds its parameters by walking its own attributes, and __call__ runs forward. A loss is just another module, and an Optimizer holds the parameter list and implements reset_grad and step.
sys250.0.9 | SYS 250 | 80 | Normalization and Regularization | Layer norm and batch norm stop activations from growing or shrinking with depth, by normalizing each layer to mean 0 and variance 1. Layer norm works across one example's features; batch norm works across the minibatch, one feature at a time, and needs running averages at test time. Regularization limits complexity: weight decay shrinks the weights by $1 - \alpha\lambda$ every step, and dropout zeroes activations with probability $p$ and scales the survivors by $1/(1-p)$. How these tricks interact is still not fully understood.
sys250.0.10 | SYS 250 | 69 | Convolutional Networks | Flattening an image into a vector wastes parameters and ignores structure. A convolution keeps the hidden layers spatial, connects each output only to a local window, and shares one filter across all positions. With channels, each filter tap is a $c_{out} \times c_{in}$ matrix. In practice this comes with zero padding, stride or pooling, groups and dilation. To differentiate it, the backward pass with respect to the input is a convolution with the flipped filter, and the backward pass with respect to the weights uses the im2col matrix.
sys250.0.11 | SYS 250 | 45 | Hardware Acceleration | Replacing numpy means understanding the hardware. The general tools are vector instructions (which need aligned memory), data layout (row-major, column-major, or strides, which make slicing, transposing and broadcasting free but can break contiguity), and parallel loops. Then the case study: matrix multiplication is still $O(n^3)$ in practice, and the speed-ups all come from reuse. Register tiling cuts DRAM loads from $2n^3$ to $n^3/v_1 + n^3/v_2$, and cache tiling adds a second level.
sys250.0.12 | SYS 250 | 44 | Lecture - 12 GPU Acceleration | A CPU spends its area on control; a GPU spends it on arithmetic, with a few commanders directing a huge number of soldiers doing the same thing. CUDA expresses that as single instruction, multiple threads: threads grouped into blocks, and blocks into a grid. Blocks map onto streaming multiprocessors with shared memory. Keep data on the GPU, have a block's threads fetch shared data into shared memory together, and tile twice (shared memory, then registers) for matrix multiplication.
sys250.0.13 | SYS 250 | 50 | Hardware Acceleration Implemention | Needle's NDArray replaces numpy. It is a flat one-dimensional handle (an aligned CPU buffer or a cudaMalloc'd GPU buffer) plus Python-side shape, strides, offset and device. Construction and arithmetic dispatch to a backend module (numpy, CPU or CUDA) that allocates an output and runs a kernel. Reshape, slice, transpose and broadcast only change shape, strides and offset. Kernels assume compact memory, so they call compact() first.
sys250.0.14 | SYS 250 | 80 | Implementing Convolutions | Three implementations of the same convolution, checked against PyTorch: a seven-deep loop (about 2,000 times slower), $K^2$ batched matrix multiplies over shifted slices (close to PyTorch), and im2col, one matrix multiply after an as_strided view unfolds every $K \times K$ window. Store images NHWC and weights $K \times K \times C_{in} \times C_{out}$, so the channel axis is last and each filter tap is a matrix.
sys250.0.15 | SYS 250 | 47 | Training Large Models | Large models are limited by GPU memory, and in training the activations dominate. The backward pass needs forward values, so the memory grows with depth. Activation checkpointing keeps only every $k$-th activation and recomputes the rest one segment at a time: with $k = \sqrt n$ memory is $O(\sqrt n)$ for about one extra forward pass. To use many GPUs, model parallelism splits the graph (with pipelining to keep workers busy) and data parallelism splits the batch and sums gradients with allreduce or a parameter server, overlapping communication with computation.
sys250.0.16 | SYS 250 | 38 | Generative Adversarial Networks | Generative modelling maps random vectors to samples, and the hard part is a loss that says whether a set of samples looks like the data and can be differentiated. A GAN learns that loss: a discriminator is trained to tell real from fake, while the generator is trained to fool it, alternating in a minimax game. Treated as a loss module, it composes with anything, as CycleGAN shows with two GAN losses and a cycle-consistency loss for unpaired image translation.
sys250.0.17 | SYS 250 | 35 | Generative Adversarial Networks Implementation | A GAN in needle, on data you can see: real points are $zA + \mu$ with $A = [[1, 2], [-0.2, 0.5]]$ and $\mu = (2, 1)$. The generator is one Linear(2, 2); the discriminator is a three-layer MLP with softmax loss. Alternating update_D and update_G moves the fake cloud onto the real one. Then the same thing is refactored into a GANLoss module, so the training loop reads like supervised learning.
sys250.0.18 | SYS 250 | 71 | Sequence Modeling and Recurrent Networks | Sequence data breaks the i.i.d. assumption: the order carries information (part-of-speech tags, speech, next-word prediction). An RNN carries a hidden state, $h_t = f(W_{hh}h_{t-1} + W_{hx}x_t + b_h)$, that can summarize everything seen so far. Autodiff trains it with backpropagation through time. In practice the state explodes or vanishes over long sequences. The LSTM's additive cell update, $c_t = c_{t-1} \odot f_t + i_t \odot g_t$, keeps information alive much longer. RNNs are also modules: stack them, run them both ways, or chain an encoder into a decoder.
sys250.0.19 | SYS 250 | 55 | RNN Implementation | An LSTM in about a dozen lines of NumPy, matched to PyTorch to numerical precision. The cell is one matrix multiply split into four gates. The layer loops the cell over time. Batching puts time first, $(T, B, n)$, so each step's slice is contiguous. Training long sequences uses truncated BPTT with hidden-state repackaging: carry the last $h$ and $c$ into the next chunk, detached.
sys250.0.20 | SYS 250 | 70 | Transformers and Attention | There are two ways to model a time series. RNNs summarize the past in a latent state: in principle unlimited history, in practice a long, fragile path. Direct prediction maps $x_{1..t}$ straight to $y_t$. Causal convolutions do that but see only a limited window. Self-attention, $\mathrm{softmax}(KQ^T/\sqrt d)V$, mixes every position with every other in one layer with no parameters of its own, at $O(T^2d)$ cost. It is permutation-equivariant, and causality has to be imposed with a mask.
sys250.0.21 | SYS 250 | 61 | Transformer Implementation | Self-attention, multi-head attention and a Transformer block in NumPy, each matched to PyTorch. Attention is one matmul to $[K\,Q\,V]$, a row-wise softmax with the mask added, times $V$, times $W_{out}$. Batching needs true batch matrix multiplication, so batch comes first. Multi-head attention reshapes $d$ into $h$ heads of $d/h$. The block adds two residuals, two layer norms and a ReLU feed-forward network.
sys250.0.22 | SYS 250 | 43 | Model Deployment | Deployment brings a trained model to phones, embedded boards and other GPUs, often without Python and with tight memory and binary size. Inference engines (TensorRT, TFLite, Core ML) interpret an exported graph (ONNX and similar) with memory reuse, fusion and lower precision, but each is a hand-built library per platform. ML compilation instead transforms an IR (fusion at the graph level, loop transformations at the kernel level) and uses automated search with a learned cost model to generate the code.
sys250.0.23 | SYS 250 | 37 | Machine Learning Compilation and Deployment Implementation | ML compilation hands-on with TVM in Colab. Write a loop program (vector add, then a 1024 × 1024 matmul) in TensorIR, build it with LLVM, call it on NDArrays, and transform it with schedule primitives (split, reorder, parallel) without rewriting the code. Tiling the matmul took it from 3.71 s to 0.37 s, and different tile sizes give different speeds, which is what automated search explores. Finally a PyTorch ResNet-18 is compiled end to end with Relay and correctly calls a cat a tabby cat.

### SYS 250 — Unit II — CUDA & Kernels (GPU MODE)
sys250.1.0 | SYS 250 | 56 | How to profile CUDA kernels in PyTorch | GPU MODE's first lecture (Mark Saroufim): how to get a custom kernel into PyTorch and how to tell whether it is any good. CUDA is asynchronous, so time with CUDA events after a warm-up and a synchronize. The autograd and PyTorch profilers show which kernels actually run. torch.utils.cpp_extension.load_inline compiles CUDA from a string. Triton is a Python alternative with an interpreter mode for debugging. torch.compile with TORCH_LOGS=output_code writes kernels you can learn from. ncu gives the hard numbers, and its hints say what to fix.
sys250.1.1 | SYS 250 | 52 | Ch1-3 PMPP book | Andreas Köpf's recap of PMPP chapters 1–3. Clock speeds stalled, so speed now comes from parallelism, and GPUs are built for throughput. CUDA programs are heterogeneous: the host allocates, copies and launches, and the device runs kernels asynchronously. A kernel is one program run by a grid of blocks of threads (at most 1,024 per block), each finding its data from blockIdx, blockDim and threadIdx, guarded against running past the end. Multi-dimensional grids map naturally onto images and matrices stored row-major.
sys250.1.2 | SYS 250 | 78 | Getting Started With CUDA for Python Programmers | Jeremy Howard's route into CUDA for Python programmers. Write the kernel first as a Python function called by a Python 'kernel runner' that loops over blocks and threads. Debug it there, have ChatGPT translate it to CUDA C, and compile it inline from a notebook. RGB to grayscale falls from about 1.5 s in Python to about 1 ms on the GPU. Matmul uses a 2-D grid of 16 × 16 blocks with one thread per output.
sys250.1.3 | SYS 250 | 57 | Compute and Memory Basics | Thomas Viehmann on PMPP chapters 4–5. An SM runs warps of 32 threads that share instruction fetch. Blocks are placed on SMs in no fixed order, and good occupancy means balancing threads, registers and shared memory while avoiding divergence and FP64. Most kernels are memory-bound, so fuse operations, estimate the 'speed of light' from bytes over bandwidth, and use the roofline to tell memory-bound from compute-bound. Tiling a matmul through shared memory cuts global reads by the tile size.
sys250.1.4 | SYS 250 | 78 | Going Further with CUDA for Python Programmers | Jeremy Howard's second lecture: using shared memory, which is about 10 times faster than global memory. A shared-memory tiled matmul is built first in Python: a runner with a shared buffer, then real threads with a threading.Barrier standing in for __syncthreads. Then it is translated to CUDA. Dynamic shared memory was mysteriously slower until the tile width was made a compile-time template parameter. The same kernel is shown in Numba too.
sys250.1.5 | SYS 250 | 68 | CUDA Performance Checklist | Mark Saroufim's CUDA performance checklist, profiled with ncu. Coalesce global memory accesses. Maximize occupancy (cudaOccupancyMaxPotentialBlockSize instead of guessing). Know whether a kernel is memory- or compute-bound from its arithmetic intensity. Minimize warp divergence. Tile reused data. Privatize. Coarsen threads. Use better maths. Latency cannot be bought, only hidden, so almost every trick is about moving fewer bytes.
sys250.1.6 | SYS 250 | 47 | Reductions | Mark Saroufim on reductions (PMPP chapter 10): operations that shrink a vector to a scalar (sum, max, mean, argmax, norms) with an identity and an associative op. On a GPU they become a tree: pair up elements, halve the active threads each step, finish in $\log_2 n$ steps. Then the kernel is improved one checklist item at a time: contiguous strides for less divergence, shared memory, multiple blocks joined by atomicAdd, thread coarsening. Floating-point order makes the result nondeterministic.
sys250.1.7 | SYS 250 | 72 | Flash Attention | Thomas Viehmann's introduction to Flash Attention: tiling applied to softmax($QK^T$)$V$ so that the $n \times n$ probability matrix is never written to memory. Each block computes one attention head. It tiles over the query rows, loops over key/value tiles, and uses the online softmax (a running maximum and running sum, rescaled when the maximum changes) to fold each tile into the output. The hard parts are keeping the output accumulators in registers and fitting within shared memory.
sys250.1.8 | SYS 250 | 82 | Practitioners Guide to Triton | Umer Adil's practitioner's guide to Triton: Python kernels compiled to PTX, operating on blocks of values rather than single threads, with shared memory managed for you. The order of reaching for tools is torch.compile, then code that compiles well, then Triton for the slow parts, then CUDA. Debug in the CPU interpreter (TRITON_INTERPRET=1). The worked examples: copy, grayscale in 2-D, naive matmul, then grouped ('super-grouped') ordering for L2 reuse, then benchmarking and autotuning.
sys250.1.9 | SYS 250 | 69 | Hacker's Guide to Speculative Decoding in VLLM | Cade Daniel on speculative decoding in vLLM. When decoding is memory-bound, a cheap proposer (a draft model, n-grams, Medusa or Eagle heads) guesses several tokens, the large model scores them all in one pass, and rejection sampling accepts a prefix. The output distribution matches the target model's exactly, and the cost of loading the weights is spread over several tokens. vLLM structures this as a spec-decode worker with proposer, scorer and verifier stages.
sys250.1.10 | SYS 250 | 77 | int8 tensorcore matmul for Turing | Erik Schultheis builds an educational int8 tensor-core matmul for Turing with only CUDA C++'s WMMA API: fragments, load_matrix_sync, mma_sync and store_matrix_sync. Integer matmul is exact, which makes testing easy. The naive 16 × 16-fragment kernel is orders of magnitude from peak. Then the standard recipe, guided by ncu's memory chart and warp-stall reasons: transpose B to column-major for coalesced loads, then register-tile 3 × 3 fragments per warp.
sys250.1.11 | SYS 250 | 86 | Mosaic GPU | Adam Paszke (PyTorch, JAX, Dex) on why Google builds Mosaic GPU and Pallas. Transformers made peak performance on a narrow class of programs the priority, and new GPUs look more and more like TPUs: huge tensor-core instructions, asynchronous copies, pipelining. So he wants a Python DSL that is tracing-based (Python control flow becomes metaprogramming) and exposes every hardware trick while removing only boilerplate. Pallas kernels take shaped, mutable refs, and BlockSpecs declare each program's tiles so copies can be pipelined automatically.

### AI 310 — Unit I — Language Modeling from Scratch (Stanford CS336, 2025)
ai310.0.0 | AI 310 | 79 | Lecture 1: Overview and Tokenization | CS336 teaches language models by building them, because the frontier has become an industry whose details are unpublished and whose behaviour changes with scale. What transfers from small models is mechanics and mindset — above all efficiency, since accuracy is efficiency times resources. The first piece built is the tokenizer, and byte-pair encoding wins because it learns its vocabulary from the corpus.
ai310.0.1 | AI 310 | 79 | Lec. 2: Pytorch, Resource Accounting | Training is resource accounting: every tensor costs bytes set by its count and data type, every matmul costs 2 × m × n × p FLOPs, and a training step costs about 6 × tokens × parameters. With those two ledgers — memory and compute — you can answer how long a run takes and how big a model fits before writing a line of model code.
ai310.0.2 | AI 310 | 87 | Lec. 3: Architectures, Hyperparameters | Modern LLMs differ less than their papers suggest: nearly all use pre-norm, most use RMSNorm, gated activations, rotary position embeddings, no bias terms, d_ff ≈ 4 d_model (8/3 for gated units), heads × head dim = d_model, and weight decay rather than dropout. Where they differ, stability and inference cost — not raw FLOPs — usually decide.
ai310.0.3 | AI 310 | 82 | Lecture 4: Mixture of experts | A mixture of experts swaps each feed-forward layer for many expert FFNs and a router that sends every token to only a few, so parameters grow while FLOPs per token stay put. The hard parts are the discrete routing decision, which can't be differentiated and is trained with heuristic balancing losses, and the instability and systems complexity that come with it.
ai310.0.4 | AI 310 | 74 | Lecture 5: GPUs | GPUs win by running a huge number of identical threads, and matrix multiplies on tensor cores are far faster than anything else — but compute has outgrown memory, so speed comes from moving less data: lower precision, fused kernels, recomputation, coalesced reads and tiling through shared memory. FlashAttention is all of these applied to attention.
ai310.0.5 | AI 310 | 80 | Lecture 6: Kernels, Triton | Measure before optimising: benchmark for end-to-end time (with warmup and synchronisation), profile to see which kernels actually run. Then the principle is the same at every level — PyTorch, CUDA, Triton or torch.compile — organise the computation to minimise reads and writes, which for elementwise and row-wise operations means fusing them into one kernel.
ai310.0.6 | AI 310 | 85 | Lecture 7: Parallelism 1 | No single GPU holds a large model or trains it fast enough, so training is split three ways: data parallelism (with ZeRO sharding its memory away), pipeline parallelism across layers, and tensor plus sequence parallelism within layers. Each spends a different scarce resource — memory, bandwidth or batch size — so real runs combine them by rule of thumb.
ai310.0.7 | AI 310 | 75 | Lecture 8: Parallelism 2 | Multi-GPU training rests on a handful of collective operations — broadcast, scatter, gather, reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter, all-reduce — that NCCL turns into packets over NVLink and NVSwitch. With them, data, tensor and pipeline parallelism each fit in a few dozen lines of PyTorch; what separates them is which tensors cross the wire and how often.
ai310.0.8 | AI 310 | 65 | Lecture 9: Scaling laws 1 | Loss falls as a power law — a straight line on a log-log plot — in data, parameters and compute, which turns design into prediction: fit small models, extrapolate to the large one. That lets you choose architectures, optimizers and the split between model size and data before spending the big budget — while remembering that compute-optimal training is not deployment-optimal.
ai310.0.9 | AI 310 | 83 | Lecture 10: Inference | Inference is a different workload from training: prefill is compute-bound, but generation produces one token at a time and is memory-bound, dominated by reading the weights and the KV cache. So the levers are reading less — smaller KV caches, quantized weights, pruned or new architectures — checking cheaply instead of generating (speculative decoding), and managing memory for ragged, dynamic traffic (continuous batching, PagedAttention).
ai310.0.10 | AI 310 | 78 | Lecture 11: Scaling laws 2 | Published scaling recipes since Chinchilla share three moves: make hyperparameters transfer across scale (muP, or fitted laws for batch size and learning rate), make the Chinchilla sweep affordable (warmup-stable-decay schedules), and size the model by IsoFLOP or joint fits. muP mostly works — but not with everything a modern LM does.
ai310.0.11 | AI 310 | 81 | Lecture 12: Evaluation | There is no one true evaluation: what you measure depends on the question — a purchase decision, raw capability, harms, or feedback for developers. Every benchmark answers four questions (inputs, how the model is called, how outputs are scored, how results are read), and each answer can quietly change what a number means.
ai310.0.12 | AI 310 | 79 | Lecture 13: Data 1 | Data is arguably the most important thing to get right, and the part developers disclose least. Pretraining corpora are built, not found: crawl or collect, convert HTML to text, filter for language and quality (by rules or by classifiers), deduplicate — every step a heuristic with consequences — and all of it under copyright law, licences and terms of service.
ai310.0.13 | AI 310 | 79 | Lecture 14: Data 2 | Filtering and deduplication are the mechanics under every dataset from the last lecture. Filtering is one framework — given a little target data T and a lot of raw data R, score R and keep what resembles T — with three instantiations (n-gram model, classifier, importance resampling) used for language, quality and toxicity alike. Deduplication at scale is hashing: exact hashes, Bloom filters, and MinHash with locality-sensitive hashing for near duplicates.
ai310.0.14 | AI 310 | 75 | Lecture 15: Alignment - SFT/RLHF | Pretraining gets you GPT-3; post-training gets you InstructGPT. The standard recipe is imitation, then optimisation: supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations extracts behaviours the base model already has, and RLHF then maximises a reward learned from pairwise preferences — first with PPO, now mostly with DPO. Both stages are only as good as their data, and both have side effects worth watching.
ai310.0.15 | AI 310 | 81 | Lecture 16: Alignment - RL 1 | RLHF cannot be scaled cleanly because a learned reward gets overoptimised. Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards sidesteps that by working where the reward is exactly what we want — is the maths answer right, do the tests pass. GRPO made it simple: PPO without the value model, with the advantage taken as a z-score within a group of rollouts. DeepSeek R1, Kimi K1.5 and Qwen 3 show the recipes, and their flaws.
ai310.0.16 | AI 310 | 76 | Lecture 17: Alignment - RL 2 | Policy gradient, worked through in code. For a language model the state is the prompt plus the response so far, the action is the next token, and the reward comes once at the end. The gradient of expected reward is just SFT weighted by reward — unbiased but noisy — and a baseline cuts the noise without changing the answer. GRPO takes its baseline from the group of responses to the same prompt; a toy sorting task shows how much each choice matters.

### AI 310 — Unit II — Finetune, Evaluate, Serve
ai310.1.0 | AI 310 | 0 | The Hugging Face LLM course — pipeline fundamentals | One call to pipeline() hides three steps — preprocess, run the model, post-process — and choosing a model is mostly choosing which half of the Transformer the task needs: an encoder to understand the whole input, a decoder to generate, or both to turn one sequence into another.
ai310.1.1 | AI 310 | 0 | Supervised finetuning in practice (TRL + alignment handbook) | Supervised fine-tuning is next-token cross-entropy on your own examples — so the decisions that matter are which tokens carry the loss, what format the data is in, and whether the end-of-sequence token matches the chat template.
ai310.1.2 | AI 310 | 0 | Quantization — GGUF, AWQ, bitsandbytes tradeoffs | Quantization buys memory with precision: the weights are stored in fewer bits and accuracy is preserved as far as the method can manage — and which method fits is decided by your hardware and by what you need to do next (load, fine-tune, compile, save), which is what the compatibility table lays out.
ai310.1.3 | AI 310 | 0 | Evals — lm-evaluation-harness, contamination, and why public benchmarks lie | The harness turns 'how good is this model?' into a reproducible command — but only if you know what the number depends on: the backend and its parallel layout, whether the model exposes logprobs, how answers were extracted, and whose prompt procedure the task follows.
ai310.1.4 | AI 310 | 0 | Serving — vLLM, PagedAttention, and the KV cache | vLLM's speed comes from treating the KV cache as managed memory — paged into fixed-size blocks, shared between requests by hashing whole prefixes, evicted least-recently-used — and its usefulness from serving all of that behind an OpenAI-compatible API.
ai310.1.5 | AI 310 | 0 | Agents — tool use, function calling, and failure modes | An LLM can only emit text, so 'tool use' is a protocol: the system prompt describes the tools, the model writes an action in an agreed format and stops, the agent parses and runs it, and the result goes back into the prompt as an observation — Thought, Action, Observation, in a loop until the task is done.
